title: How to look at your data — Jeff Huber (Chroma) + Jason Liu (567)

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 96%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is evaluation methodology: fast evals for retrieval, empirical embedding model comparison, and conversation output analysis frameworks. The evaluation and analysis methods are applicable to any AI application with retrieval or conversation data, not specific to a vertical. Fast evals address the evaluation stage, while conversation analysis and the decision quadrant support ongoing production monitoring. Assumes familiarity with retrieval systems, embeddings, and basic data analysis but does not require advanced technical depth. A two-part conference presentation with case studies and live demonstrations. All supporting evidence is directly stated in the transcript with said_in_transcript grade anchors.

summary: Jeff Huber opens by emphasizing that AI practitioners should "look at your data" to systematically improve retrieval systems rather than guessing or relying on slow LLM-as-judge evaluations. He introduces "fast evals": sets of query-document pairs (a golden data set) where queries are run against the system to measure whether expected documents are retrieved. These evals are fast and inexpensive, enabling many rapid experiments. When queries are unavailable, LLMs can be taught to write realistic synthetic queries; naive generation produces overly clean, overly specific queries unlike real-world data. Chroma published research showing they could semantically align synthetic query specificity to real user queries. A Weights & Biases chatbot case study evaluated four embedding models using recall at 10, comparing ground-truth logged queries against synthetic ones. Findings: the originally used text-embedding-3-small performed worst; Gina embeddings v3 (top on MTeB for English) underperformed for this application; Voyage 3 Large performed best — empirically determined, not guessed. All code is open source. Jason Liu then shifts to analyzing outputs, particularly conversation histories from agents and chatbots. For small volumes, manual review is best; only use LLMs when you believe they're smarter than you. At scale, the approach is to extract structured metadata from conversations (summaries, topics, tools, errors, frustration), embed it, cluster to identify segments, and test hypotheses — analogous to marketing segmentation. He introduces Cura, a library that summarizes conversations, clusters them, builds cluster hierarchies, and compares eval KPIs across segments. This reveals patterns like factuality being low for time-filter queries but high for contract search. Liu presents a decision quadrant combining usage volume (high/low) with eval performance (high/low): high usage and low performance means you must fix it; high usage and high performance is fine; low usage and high performance suggests product education; low usage and low performance may just need a prompt deflection. A key insight is that solutions often involve adding infrastructure (e.g., a time filter, an OCR step) rather than improving the AI itself. The ultimate goal is a data-driven product roadmap where impact-weighted analysis — e.g., knowing 40% of conversations involve data visualization — justifies targeted investments. Huber's takeaways emphasize avoiding public benchmarks, building evals on your own data, focusing first on retrieval (since LLM improvements won't fix bad retrieval), using synthetic data when lacking users, and always looking at both inputs and outputs.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the Case for Looking at Your Data
sections.summary: Jeff Huber introduces the two-part talk, emphasizes everything is open source, and states the core hypothesis: you should look at your data. He argues you can only manage what you measure, and great measurement makes systematic improvement easy.

sections.title: Fast Evals for Retrieval Systems
sections.summary: Huber defines fast evals as sets of query-document pairs (golden data sets) that run quickly and inexpensively, enabling rapid experimentation. He contrasts this with guess-and-check, slow LLM-as-judge frameworks, and public benchmarks like MTeB.

sections.title: Generating Realistic Synthetic Queries
sections.summary: Huber explains that LLMs can be taught to write queries, but naive generation produces overly clean, overly specific questions unlike real-world data. Chroma developed methods to semantically align synthetic query specificity to real user queries.

sections.title: Weights & Biases Chatbot Case Study
sections.summary: Huber presents a case study evaluating four embedding models on the W&B chatbot using recall at 10, comparing ground-truth vs synthetic queries. Text-embedding-3-small performed worst, Gina embeddings v3 (MTeB leader) underperformed, and Voyage 3 Large performed best.

sections.title: Jason Liu: Analyzing Conversation Outputs
sections.summary: Jason Liu shifts to output analysis. For small volumes, manual review is best; only use LLMs when you believe they're smarter than you. At scale, extract structured metadata from conversations, cluster to identify segments, and test hypotheses — drawing an analogy to marketing audience segmentation for actionable decision-making.

sections.title: Cura Library and the Analysis Pipeline
sections.summary: Liu introduces Cura, a library for summarizing conversations, clustering them, building hierarchies, and comparing eval KPIs across segments. He references Anthropic Cleo's finding that code use was 40x more represented by Claude users than GDP value creation. He demonstrates the pipeline with fake Gemini conversations, extracting topics, frustrations, and errors, then clustering into groups like data visualization, SEO content, and authentication errors, and grouping into higher-level themes like technical support.

sections.title: Decision Framework: Usage × Performance Quadrant
sections.summary: Liu presents a decision quadrant combining usage volume (high/low) with eval performance (high/low). High usage and low performance means you must fix it; high usage and high performance is fine; low usage and high performance suggests education or product changes; low usage and low performance may just need a prompt deflection. He emphasizes that solutions often involve infrastructure (time filters, OCR steps, new tools) rather than AI improvements. After segmentation, you can build intent classifiers, routers, and monitoring across categories.

sections.title: Takeaways and Resources
sections.summary: Huber and Liu summarize key takeaways: for inputs, avoid public benchmarks, build evals on your data, focus on retrieval first since LLM improvements won't fix bad retrieval, and use synthetic data when lacking users. For outputs, extract structure from conversations, do population-level analysis, find clusters, and build impact-weighted understanding. They share QR codes for Chroma cloud research and three Jupyter notebooks demonstrating the full process with W&B conversations.

sections.title: Q&A: Spicy Take on Pricing
sections.summary: During a brief Q&A, Liu shares a spicy take: agent businesses should price their services on work done or value delivered rather than tokens used.
